steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The winter the sea took the bell, Elias stopped speaking to anyone but the light.

The bell had hung from the iron framework below the gallery since before he was born, a rust-flecked tongue that tolled when fog rolled in and the horn machinery seized, or when storms shook the tower hard enough to make its cables sing. His father said the bell knew the names of ships, his mother said it knew the names of the dead, and Elias, who’d been born in the keeper’s cottage at the foot of the lighthouse and had learned his letters from weather logs, liked both explanations equally.

He heard it go in the middle of the night.

The storm arrived without the usual prelude of days-long swells and a slow thickening of the horizon. One moment the sea was calm as slate, the next it reared up, pale and streaked, under lightning that seemed to tear the sky on its hinges. The wind turned from a howl into a blunt, hammering roar, pushing at the tower from new directions, as if the storm were circling, looking for a way in.

Elias woke already halfway out of bed, his body moving before his mind caught up, the way years of repetition had trained him. Seventeen steps down from the small iron cot to the watch room, check the lantern fuel, check the wick height, make sure the lens rotation had not lost its pace. Then up, up, the narrow stone staircase spiraling around the hollow center of the tower like the grooves of a shell.

He counted the steps as he climbed. He always did. Ninety-eight from the cottage door to the lantern room, a comforting span of numbers that felt as unchangeable as the tides. Tonight, they were off. Or his breathing was. Or the tower itself, vibrating under blasts of wind that hit like cannon shots.

When he reached the gallery, the storm hit him full in the face. The door wrenched out of his hand and slammed against the stone, the safety chain the only thing keeping it from flying clear into the dark. Rain slammed sideways, hard enough to sting, and the wind grabbed at the edges of his oilskin coat like rough hands.

He should have gone back in, shut himself in the glass womb of the lantern room, but habit carried him along the slick outer walk, one hand on the rail. He wanted to see if the bell’s cable had tangled again, or if the storm had loosened any of the iron bolts. The old keeper—his father, before the accident—had walked this same circle in storms worse than this, or so the family stories said. Elias had never been able to tell if those stories were meant as warnings or challenges.

Lightning crackled, close enough that the metal railing hummed under his palm. Revealed in that white glare, for a second, was the sea: not a surface, but a thousand live things, each wave a separate beast, all of them shouldering and snarling at the rocks around the headland. The bell cable cut like a line of ink through the light, stretched taut as a bowstring.

Then came the sound: not the bell itself, but the shriek of metal giving way.

One of the anchor bolts that had held the bell frame to the masonry tore free. The wind caught the bell like a toy, swinging it out, slamming it back. Elias felt the railing lurch, and for a heartbeat he thought the entire gallery might rip from the tower. He dropped to one knee automatically, bracing.

The bell swung once more, wildly. Its clapper struck the side only as it spun, not in its practiced measured toll, but an awkward, jangling blow. A maimed sound, half clang and half scream, cut off at once as the last bolt snapped.

The bell, its frame, and a long length of cable spun away into the dark. There was no splash, not audible over the storm. Just absence, and the wind in its place.

Elias stared into the black where it had gone, though there was nothing to see. Lightning did not oblige him a second revelation. The sea poured and surged and climbed the rocks, anonymous once more.

He did not tell the light the bell was gone. The light already knew.

In the morning, the world looked as if nothing had happened. The storm had spent itself hours before dawn, and now a pearl-colored fog draped lightly over the water, thin enough to taste of salt on the tongue yet not thick enough to hide the company of waves. The gulls were back on their rocks, grumbling. The air smelled of kelp and broken shells.

The gallery’s stone rim bore a fresh white scar where the frame had torn free. When he leaned over and looked down, carefully, with one hand gripped tight to the railing, he could see where the cable had scored the side of the tower, leaving a twisted black track. The bell itself was nowhere. Even in the most sheltered folds of rock around the headland, no shape broke the foam—a small mercy, he thought. He had not wanted to see it lying broken, mute and barnacled.

Losing the bell meant paperwork. Calls on the radio, yet another letter of explanation to the Manager in the town, a request for a replacement that would probably be filed into a stack and forgotten. The foghorn machinery had been repaired last year, after enough complaints; in theory, the bell was redundant. In theory, everything important could be done from shore now. That was what they said, the men who came out twice a year with clipboards and little masks of polite disinterest on their faces.

“The light is automatic,” one had said, on the last inspection visit, standing stiffly in the watch room with his polished boots discreetly avoiding the rust-stain where Elias’s father’s boots had always stood. “The rotation, the fuel, all of it. You’re here as a redundancy, Mr. Kellan. Systems fail, after all.”

Elias had thought of telling him that some systems were failing already, that the cracks in the stone on the landward side were widening each winter, that the cottage roof had begun to weep during the last heavy rain. Instead, he had said that the light was more than its mechanisms.

“Of course,” the inspector had replied, glancing at his watch. “Tradition, and so on.”

Elias had not bothered to correct him.

He went back through the lantern room and down, counting the steps again. They felt wrong beneath his feet, as if some invisible transfer of weight had changed the balance of the entire tower when the bell left.

At forty, the turning of the stairs opened into the small alcove where the radio sat. He paused. The storm had passed; the channels would be clearer now.

“Kellan Light, this is Kellan Light, reporting structural loss,” he said when the familiar crackle of the Manager’s line came through. His voice sounded flat to his own ears, like a recording of itself. “The auxiliary bell and frame were sheared off during the night storm. No other damage observed.”

The pause felt longer than it was. He pictured the Manager down in the square little office at the harbor, the one with framed paintings of lighthouses lining the walls and stacks of shipping reports on his desk.

“The bell’s gone?” the Manager said. “Sheared off?”

“Yes.”

“Any injuries?”

“No, sir.”

“Good. I’ll fill out the loss report.” A rustle of papers, a mutter that might have been numbers. “The foghorn’s working fine, yes? And the lantern?”

“Yes. All operational.”

“All right. We’ll requisition a new bell, though it may be a while. Budget’s thin this year. You’ve got the horn, you should be fine.”

Elias did not say that the ships knew the bell’s voice, that fishermen out beyond the headland could tell, in a storm, when they were abreast of Kellan by its tone alone. He did not say that the bell had marked, for every keeper before him, the thinness of the world in fog: the damp press of air that blurred distance, the way each toll seemed to fall not just over the sea but into some hollow under the tower, far below the foundations.

“Understood,” he said.

“And, Elias? Might be we’ll be changing your status come spring. There’s talk of shifting Kellan to full automation, making you part-time. We’ll discuss it when the board decides anything concrete.”

The line clicked as the Manager passed his hand over the mouthpiece, muffling his next words as he turned his head. Elias heard something like “modernize” and “cost-effective” before the sound cleared again.

“That’s not decided yet,” the Manager finished. “We’ll talk. Carry on.”

Elias clicked off without replying. The radio hissed into empty static, then quiet.

Full automation. Part-time. Words that had been circling the tower for years, floating in on the same currents as the gulls, the driftwood, and the occasional plastic crate. He had never imagined they’d snag here.

When you spend your life watching the horizon, you get used to distant threats. Storm lines, marching across the dark. The low bloom of thunder. Lights of some drunken captain steering too close. Elias had always trusted that he would see what was coming in time to brace against it.

He had not expected the danger to arrive on a folded sheet of paper, carried out, when it came, by a young courier who smelled of city soap and said “Sir” as if it were a curious old word he’d learned in a book.

The letter didn’t come that day, not yet. For several days after the storm, nothing came but rain.

Elias found, in the new quiet—without the bell’s familiar, occasional rattle—to talk more to the light.

He had always done it, since boyhood, in the private tongue of mutters and glances and small, practical endearments. “Easy, now,” when the wick flared on first lighting. “Steady,” when the lens shrieked faintly against its worn bearings. His father had spoken to it too, though less; his father had spoken more to the logbooks and the barometer, to the little silver compass on the wall that he polished every Sunday with a bit of cloth.

Now the words came more freely.

“You’d think they’d know better than to take you down to part-time,” he said one evening, as he cleaned the salt haze from the inside of the lantern glass. The wind had turned east, bringing a sift of fine crystals that dried white and cloudy where they hit. “Storms don’t work on a schedule.”

The light did not answer, of course. It sat in its center of glass and brass and steel, the Fresnel lens the color of an old wine bottle, its many ranks of glass prisms bending and focusing his reflection as he moved: Elias in slices, elongated and bent, one eye large and one small.

“I know, I know,” he said to that stretched, fractured face. “You’ll go on. They’ll wire you in from the town, keep you on a timer. Maybe they’ll put you on a weather sensor, wake you when the fog thickens. No need of a keeper walking the stones, checking the oil, listening. No need of eyes, so long as the bulb burns.”

He finished the cleaning, checked the rotation weight, listened to the slow, healthy tick of the escapement that kept the lens turning at its stately, precise pace. In all important ways, nothing had changed.

Below, in the cottage, the changes showed more clearly.

His father’s boots had stayed in their corner, as if his father might yet be coming back from that last walk to the cliffs. His pipe lay on the mantel, the last smudge of ash in its bowl as neat as if it had been set down for a momentary interruption. The chair by the window, the one that looked west, took his absence into its cushions, hollowing slowly under no one’s weight.

The house lived off lists. Times of meals. Times of lightings. Times of checks, written by his father’s hand, then his, in the little notebook that hung from a nail in the kitchen. “04:00 – Wake. 04:30 – Inspect fuel supply. 05:00 – Walk perimeter.”

After the bell went, he added a line one morning: “05:30 – Listen.”

He did not know what he meant until that first grey dawn, with the fog horn silent and the sea lying in a deceptive calm, when he stood on the rocks below the tower and cupped a hand around his ear as if that could help him catch some other sound.

The absence of the bell had made a hole. Just there, at the edge of hearing, before the waves and after the wind, a particular hollow note waited to be filled. Now it filled itself with different things: the clink of pebble against pebble as the outgoing waves drew them down-slope, the far, croaking bark of seals. Once, faintly, he thought he heard voices.

He knew the tricks of sound over water. You could hear a conversation on a trawler a mile out as clearly as if the men were standing beside you, if the air lay right and if the sea didn’t argue. He’d heard laughter, once, and shared it without knowing the joke. He’d heard a man singing, high and hoarse, some hymn Elias’s mother used to hum under her breath while she kneaded bread.

These sounds were not like that. They were not coming from any direction he recognized. If anything, they were coming from below.

He crouched, then, closer to the water, one hand braced on the slick rock, ignoring the cold creeping through his trousers. The voices—not words, not yet, just the shape of them—rose and fell in a rhythm that prickled the hair on his arms.

When the next wave slid back, there between the kelp ribbons and the barnacled rock, he saw the bell.

It lay on its side in a hollow the sea had scoured, its frame twisted and half-buried in a spill of shingle. The long cable, stripped of its outer casing, splayed like seaweed. The bell’s metal had dulled from its old, patched bronze to a greenish-brown, as if weeks had passed instead of days.

He should not have been able to see it. The spot where it lay was under the overhang of the cliff, where the waves plunged and reversed in white chaos. But there, for that moment between the rush and the return, the water thinned and cleared, and the bell’s mouth gaped up at him, dark and waiting.

The voices came again, thin and far away, as if someone were speaking through a long, echoing corridor.

He jerked back, his boots slipping. For a long second he did not trust his own eyes. Then the next wave came in, slapped the rock, roared, foamed, and when it went out the hollow under the cliff looked as it always had: rock, weed, shadow. No bell.

Elias went back up the path, his breath loud in his ears. He did not look for the bell again.

But after that, he heard it sometimes, under the water, under the wind. A hollow dong, slow and out of rhythm with his remembered pattern, resonant and thick. Once, waking in the small hours, he heard it distinctly, as if someone had struck a bell right below his bed. His heart had slammed once, hard enough that he’d had to sit up and put his hand flat on his chest, feeling the echo.

“You miss it too,” he told the light.

The light burned steadily, its rotation throwing long, slow spokes over the dark water. It did not flicker.

It was in that same week that the courier came with the letter about automation.

He arrived in one of the harbor’s small motorboats, the spray from its bow throwing a faint, crystalline rainbow in the autumn sun. The gulls followed him in, thinking perhaps that he was a fisherman. Elias was on the gallery, finishing the midday lens check, and saw the boy—he was hardly more than that, slender and pale under his orange lifejacket—climb the narrow iron ladder up from the landing ledge with stiff-armed care.

“Mr. Kellan?” he called when he reached the top of the stairs.

“That’s my father,” Elias said, then caught himself, that reflexive correction hanging in the air. “Elias is fine.”

The boy held out an envelope. His fingers were reddened from the climb and the cold.

“From the Harbor Office, sir. They said it was urgent.”

The paper was already damp at the edges, the ink in the corners of the typed address smearing faintly. Elias turned away from the wind as he slit it open with his thumbnail.

The letter inside was brief, written in the curt, careful phrases of an administrative template with the blanks filled in. Review of operations, modernization initiative, budget considerations. Effective date. Reassignment.

His stipend would be halved. His presence would be required only during certain hours, on certain days—“to perform routine maintenance tasks not suited to automated systems”—and at other times the light would be monitored remotely by the harbor’s new surveillance center.

“This will ensure the continued safe operation of Kellan Light while bringing it in line with modern operational standards,” the letter concluded. “Your years of service are recognized and appreciated. We look forward to discussing the transition with you at your earliest convenience.”

He read it twice, the second time more slowly, as if the words might shift into something else under sustained attention. They did not.

“Sir?” the courier said. “They asked if I could take back a signed copy, receipt of notice. If that’s all right.”

Elias looked at him. The boy’s eyes darted past him, over the rail, out to the day. The sea lay bright and calm, the light’s shadow a faint, gleaming path stretching westward.

From up here, the mainland looked like a painting: green and gold fields, the tuck of the harbor, the smear of smoke from some small fire. From there, perhaps, Kellan was just a slender shape of stone on the horizon, a marker, nothing more.

“They’ll be watching you from there, now,” Elias said, to nobody in particular.

“Sir?” the boy repeated.

He signed the receipt.

After the courier left, the boat’s engine dwindling into a faint, insect whine, Elias folded the letter along its creases and put it in the drawer with the weather logs.

Then he climbed, as he always did, to the lantern room.

“They’re going to make you watch yourself,” he told the light. “Cameras, sensors, radios. They’ll put a little red mark on a screen that blinks if you falter. Someone on a night shift in a warm room will tap a key, send you a message, and if you don’t answer they’ll send a boat. Or not, if the budget’s thin that month.”

His voice scratched in his throat. He had never thought of himself as someone who would cry over a letter. He did not cry now, but something in his chest felt tight, compacted like wet rope wound too many times around the same post.

“I’ve been the one to watch you,” he said. “My father before me. His mother, before him. We’ve brought you oil and polished your glass and checked your gears. We’ve known, by your sound, when you were happy and when something was wrong.
